medium: Pencil on a spiral-bound sketchbook page; the heading in a darker, finer line
provenance: Drawn by Larry from memory on 2026-09-12, during the sitting in which he commented on the camp, flight-line and mountain photographs that day. He offered to draw it; his son did not ask. His son calls it the flight line and the airport. His son scanned the sheet flat with a phone the same afternoon (a one-page PDF, Scan_20260912_150027 Ton Son Nhut Airport.pdf, 15:00, kept in the archive as it arrived; the filename is his son’s) and sent it to the archive; the sheet stays with the family. The image shown is the page taken out of the PDF without re-encoding. The heading is drawn in a darker, finer line than the pencil labels, and his son confirms that Larry wrote it. Not recorded: whether he was looking at any photograph while he drew, the order in which he drew and labelled things, and anything he said as he drew.
title: Flight line, “Ton Son Nhut”
description: A plan drawn on a sketchbook page, shown with the spiral binding along the top. Near the top, the word RUNWAY is written above a long horizontal line that runs across most of the page. Below it, in a darker and finer line than the rest of the sheet, a heading runs across the upper centre: the words TON SON NHUT followed by a third word, which is not transcribed because one of its letters cannot be read with confidence. Below the heading are several short, faint horizontal strokes, and at the far left, under RUNWAY, a short diagonal stroke and a small hooked mark. At the left of the page, standing on a second long line that crosses the page to its right edge, are three small aircraft, each with writing above it. The left-hand one is heavily crossed through, under three characters, two rounded shapes and a figure like a 7, which are not transcribed. The middle one is a high-winged aeroplane with a propeller and wheels, under a word beginning BEAV that is not transcribed because one of its letters cannot be read with confidence. The right-hand one is a smaller cross-shaped aeroplane under L19. At the right edge, above the second line, a vertical line is crossed by five short horizontal strokes, with a small loop at its top and faint marks between the strokes. Below the second line, two long vertical lines run close together down the page a little right of centre. Left of them is a box with two lines of writing, not transcribed because letters in both lines cannot be read with confidence. Right of them is a large box labelled HANGER, with a second line of writing below it whose first two words are US POST; its third word has a letter that cannot be read with confidence, so the line is left out whole. At the bottom, left of the vertical lines, is a box with two lines of writing, USAF above a line ending in HALL; one letter of the word before HALL cannot be read with confidence, so the inscription is left out whole. At the bottom right is a small box labelled MOVIE’S. Nothing on the sheet indicates scale or compass direction.
researchNotes: Drawn the day he placed the flight line in words at the photographs: “At the flight line probably 3 blocks away. There was a Beaver airplane” (VN-0012), “Just taking off on the flight line heading to Nui Ba Den” (VN-0016), and “this is the Flight Line” (VN-0020). The heading repeats TON SON NHUT as he wrote it on VD-0001 a week earlier, the same rendering in his hand twice. It names the airfield as he remembers it and is not evidence of where it was; the identification with Tân Sơn Nhứt stays a hypothesis on the place record. L-19 was the Army’s designation for the Cessna Bird Dog until 1962, when it became the O-1; on the sheet L19 is written above a drawing of an aeroplane. The crossed-through aircraft and the characters above it, the untranscribed boxes, the ladder-like mark at the right edge, and the two close vertical lines are not interpreted here; they are his to explain. The sheet gives no distances, so it does not bear on where his hooch stood relative to the flight line.
